subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF LETTER FROM PREMIER BULGANIN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs or the Acting Prime Minister. I would like to ask him if he has tabled or will now table a copy of the letter reported in the press this morning as having been received yesterday by the government, through the Prime Minister, from Mr. Bulganin of Russia, so the house may have the letter as well as the press information.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF LETTER FROM PREMIER BULGANIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the letter addressed to the Prime Minister from Premier Bulganin was delivered yesterday afternoon by the Soviet ambassador. The letter was in Russian and was accompanied by what was described as an unofficial embassy translation. The note is now being translated and studied, and any comment by the government would have to await this careful examination.
The principal features of the note have been published in the papers this morning. For the most part it resembles the letters sent to President Eisenhower, Prime Minister Macmillan and others.
There are, however, a few passages specifically referring to Canada. The proposals in the note will undoubtedly be given careful consideration at the NATO council meeting in Paris, and I hope to be able to table the translation the first of the week.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF LETTER FROM PREMIER BULGANIN
speechtext: I notice that the Prime Minister has already commented on the note. Could we receive the comment as well, since the note is characterized as propaganda by the Prime Minister?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF LETTER FROM PREMIER BULGANIN
speechtext: I think the comment must have been made on the basis of this unofficial translation by the Russian embassy. There has as yet been no official translation by the Department of External Affairs.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the clause which continues to leave a rate of taxation on the first $1,000 of income over the present exemption levels of $1,000 for a single person and $2,000 for a married person. As the committee is well aware, we argued yesterday, and in fact we put it before the house in the form of a motion, that the least that should now be done would be for that rate to be diminished. It is still our view that the party now in power should carry out the policy which it had when it was on this side of the house, namely that there should be no income tax on the first $1,000 of income over the present exemption level; in other words that these exemption levels should be increased.
The minister has sought to dispel the idea that the Conservative party promised to raise the exemption levels. He made the statement last night, that the Prime Minister did not make such a promise, and every time it has been contended from this side of the house that this was the position of the party now in power, we have been given to understand that we were twisting the record. Well, I may say that I have gone through the record. I do not intend this morning to take the time of the house to quote all that I have found, but I may say that over the past number of years there have been repeated occasions when members of the Conservative party have stood up in this house and said they were in favour of raising the exemption levels to $1,500 for single persons and $3,000 for married persons.
Some of those hon. members might now be described as backbenchers, who were not necessarily speaking for the party. I do not think, however, that their statements can be dismissed, especially when they were made by such persons as the former member for Hastings-Frontenac, now appointed to another place. I do not think the words of the present Secretary of State can be dismissed. She argued quite definitely on more than one occasion that the exemptions should be raised to $1,500 single and $3,000 married.
But, Mr. Chairman, let me quote from the record of Hansard the exact words of no less a person than the hon. member for Eglinton, now Minister of Finance. I am looking at page 474 of Hansard for January 24, 1956. Let it be perfectly clear, as it will be from the sentences I will read, that the present Minister of Finance was not just speaking for himself. He seldom did when he was on this side of the house. He always spoke for the party, and he made it clear on that occasion that that was what he was doing. He was speaking in the debate on the address on January 24, 1956. When he referred to

Income Tax Act
the minister of finance he was, of course, referring to Mr. Walter Harris, who held the portfolio at that time. These were the words of the present Minister of Finance:
If the Minister of Finance is not prepared to go as far as Conservative policy advocates-
The word "Conservative" is printed with a capital C, so it was not just an idea of the hon. member for Eglinton; he was telling us what was the policy of his party.
If the Minister of Finance is not prepared to go as far as Conservative policy advocates in this respect, namely $1,500 for single persons and $3,000 for married persons without dependants, then at least we hope he will take a generous step in that direction.
This, Mr. Chairman, is a clear cut statement by the present Minister of Finance, when he was in opposition, as to where his party stood. Later in the same session- this was last year, 1956, on July 3-we were debating the amendments to the Income Tax Act, the very stage at which we now find ourselves, and the present Minister of Finance condemned Mr. Harris for not having done what he, the hon. member for Eglinton, had called upon him to do on January 24, namely for not having raised the exemption levels as had been demanded by representatives of the Progressive Conservative party. I may say that the words of the present Minister of Finance in that session were not uttered by him as one lone voice crying in the Conservative wilderness, but were supported by those whom I have already named, as well as by others.
Now, Mr. Chairman, anyone who takes the index to Hansard, looks up the Income Tax Act, and then looks down until he comes to the word "exemptions" can find there in the pages of Hansard across the years representatives of the Conservative party advocating that exemption levels should be raised and, in specific terms, that they should be raised to $1,500 single and $3,000 married.
When, against such a background, the leader of a party, particularly the hon. gentleman who is now Prime Minister, goes into an election campaign and promises there will be tax cuts, promises that there will be given back to the people the $10 a month by which, he said, they were being overtaxed, I say the Canadian people had every right to believe that was the Prime Minister's way of saying that the Conservative policy indicated in the House of Commons by the present Minister of Finance would be implemented.
I am going to avoid making any reference to newspaper reports of what the Prime Minister said, because he is not here in this house to confirm or deny the accuracy of such reports, but I do want to read one or two quotations from statements he made over the
[Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) .1
C.B.C., in this case over a radio hook-up. He made similar statements on television as well. Speaking from Vancouver on May 24, 1957, the present Prime Minister said:
We shall put an end to excessive overtaxation. We shall call a session of parliament in September to reduce taxes, and at that session, with $500 million of overtaxation last year, we will be able to increase old age pensions and other pensions to fair and reasonable amounts. The Liberals tell you it is not possible to lower taxes and increase pensions at the same time. Give us a chance-we will show you!
We have.

Now, Mr. Chairman, I think it is time something pretty straight was said about the political morality of a party which takes one stand when it is on one side of the house and another stand when it is on the other side. I think I could choose words of my own to express what people think about this kind of political morality, but I will forbear. I will quote instead a recognized authority, one that is certainly recognized by my hon. friends opposite in view of the ways in which they seem to be copying some of the things he did. I refer to the late Viscount Bennett, who at the time he made the remarks I shall now read was the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, Conservative prime minister of Canada. He did not call himself a Progressive Conservative, he was just a straight Conservative. Some say he was a Liberal-Conservative, but I cannot keep track of all these changes in party names.
There was nothing Liberal about him.
He did not belong to the C.C.F. anyway.

speechtext: Someone said he did not belong to the C.C.F.; we know that.

speechtext:
However, the same Mr. Bennett tried on his political deathbed to bring in some progressive legislation. We know what happened to it, and now when we try to bring back some of that progressive legislation you know what happens to it on the floor of this house.
These were the remarks of Mr. Bennett on the subject of the political morality of people changing their views when they move from one side of the house to the other. He was speaking on July 27, 1931, as reported at page 4200 of Hansard for that year. It is true that he was directing his fire at the Liberals for having changed their views on moving from the government side to the opposition side, but as hon. members will see Mr. Bennett's words apply with equal force to those who move from the opposition side to the government side. These were the words of Mr. Bennett:
I must say that I do not believe the Canadian people think it is necessary for political leaders who one day are in power and the next day are in opposition to revile when in opposition all that they held most dear when they were in power, to change their ground, to shift their position and say, "That which I asked you to accept I now ask you to condemn; that which I told you I believed

in then I no longer believe in. I misled you when I told you to do thus and so, not knowing whether X knew or not; I instructed you right then, but now, with changed conditions all that is wrong, all that is nonsense, all that is absurd. What I want to do now is to condemn this thing."
Those are Mr. Bennett's words, and I apply them directly to a party whose present Minister of Finance said in this house last year that it was Conservative policy to raise exemption levels to $1,500 single and $2,000 married, to a party whose leader in the election campaign said, "Give this party a chance and we will raise pensions and reduce taxes; we will put back into your pockets that $10 a month which the Liberals were overcharging you." This is a party that now having gone to the other side of the house, when we propose these things follows a course of action such as we have had in this house in the last day or so, of doing its best to avoid even having to face votes on amendments designed to implement the very things that members of that party said they stood for when they were in opposition and when they were out on the hustings.
I insist, Mr. Chairman, that the Canadian people do not like this sort of thing. It is most disillusioning. Some of the things that have happened here lately at the instigation of those who a year ago were talking about the dignity of parliament and respect for the chair are disillusioning to the people of this country. And what this minister is trying to do right now, in saying that his party did not promise to raise these exemption levels, and asking us to settle for these rates of tax that still apply to the low income people that the Conservatives condemned the Liberals for taxing, is the kind of political morality that merits the condemnation that Mr. Bennett indicated back in 1931 in those words I quoted. It is still the case under this clause that three million people, who in the words of the Conservatives have been overtaxed $10 a month, are on their own terms still being overtaxed at least $7.50 a month.
Those are not my words, and those are not my figures. That is the ground the present party in power chose for election purposes. That is the ground upon which we have the right to judge them in this house at the present time. Of course we welcome the reduction of $2.50 in the taxes on these three million people, but I say to the party opposite that they will be held to account not merely for the policies they bring into the house or fail to bring into the house, but will also be held to account for political morality of this type.

The fact is, sir, that to put into effect an increase to $1,500 in the basic exemption for single persons and $3,000 for married persons would cost the treasury of this country approximately $530 million, and that kind of money was not available in the balance of ways and means within the scope of the budget that was passed at the last session of the house before dissolution.
I have said it there and there is no point in my attempting to repeat it now. That is the position; that is the fact, and having regard to what my hon. friend has said concerning views expressed by myself and other members of my party when in opposition, there has been no departure from those views.
We would like nothing better than to be in a position to proceed now to put such figures into effect but we have to accept the situation, and in this bill we have done what we asked the former government to do. Mr. Speaker, before the bill is given third reading there are one or two points that I believe should receive further consideration in the house. Earlier this morning I got an answer from the Minister of Finance with respect to what the bill will cost the treasury in respect of those in receipt of taxable incomes of over $2,000 per year. The minister stated, as I heard him, that there were approximately one and a half million taxpayers in this category. My arithmetic suggests that that figure multiplied by $30 comes to a total of $45 million per year. When the minister replied last night to my original question he had this to say, as found at page 2364 of Hansard.
Mr. Chairman, it would be an entirely new theory of progressive taxation to say that when you get above the level of $2,000 of taxable income you are not going to tax everybody in the same way on his initial $2,000 of taxable income. That would be an entirely new theory.
Under most circumstances I probably would be quite willing to agree fully with that statement of the minister. However, I think we should realize that the effect of the bill, as the result of the consideration that has been given to it, falls far short of what the people of Canada were led to expect would be done by a Conservative administration, and that in the absence of a basic increase in the exemptions perhaps the consistency to which the minister refers is not as desirable as might have been the case under some other circumstances.
I think point is lent to the suggestion in the minister's statement that you tax everybody in the same way, by the features of the bill having to do with the rebate or allowance for board and lodging of construction workers. If the minister is going to hold himself out as championing the taxing of everybody in the same way in one clause of the bill, and then is going to ignore that principle completely in another clause of the bill, I think his consistency is very much open to question, to say the least. The minister has tried to suggest that the proposal

with respect to construction workers is a new and radical departure in legislation. As found at page 2327 of Hansard he said:
. . . at no time in the consideration of this matter has any question been raised as to any other persons.
I do not believe the bill should be allowed to pass without the attention of the house again being drawn to the fact that the question of allowing exemptions for board, lodging and travelling expenses in the case of workers who, because of their employment, have to live away from their regular homes has been brought up and considered many times in the house. Consideration was given to that matter by the house long before the question of this administrative bulletin No. 10 of the Department of National Revenue was ever brought up.
It is true that a good deal of furore arose across the country because certain groups of people were having certain concessions taken away from them, but I hope the minister understands that people may be a lot more vocal in their objections when they suddenly have something taken away from them which they have enjoyed than if they are attempting to secure the removal of certain discriminations and given something which they have not enjoyed before. I hope the Minister of Finance is not going to allow this subject to get shoved into the back corner of his mind somewhere and forget about it. If the minister is going to use the words he used last night in discussing clause 3, to the effect that everyone would be taxed in the same way, then those words are not going to be forgotten.
In discussing clause 1 the minister had something to say about the interpretation that would be placed upon this clause. At page 2328 of Hansard for December 13, 1957, he said:
I can only say to him-
He was replying to a question asked by the hon. member for Cartier.
-that the interpretation will be a matter tor the Department of National Revenue, and having regard to the purpose of the clause I am quite satisfied that the department will endeavour to place a fair and ample interpretation upon it.
Now, we are faced with the position that this legislation is going to pass out of the hands of the Minister of Finance, who is introducing it, and into the hands of another department. I hope the Minister of Finance will see to it that the Department of National Revenue understands the wording of this clause. For example, I would suggest that he make sure that the Department of National Revenue realizes that the words
Income Tax Act
"construction worker" should not be interpreted in such a way as to apply only to employees of construction companies.

I do not think the government should be satisfied that the bill now before the house, coupled with any other policy that it has announced to date, will be in fact sufficient to do the job. The truth is that we have a vast surplus of grain in this country which is a burden to the nation. One reason is that money is being paid out of the consolidated revenue fund toward the cost of storage and interest charges, but it is also a burden on the country because producers have to keep large quantities of grain on their farms and they must maintain buildings to house that grain, which is an extremely expensive proposition for them.
There is great need, in fact there is urgent need, to increase by a vast amount Canada's exports of grain. If we are timid in our attitude and in our policies as a country, and if we allow these large surpluses to remain in Canada, it is only a matter of time until we will have lost the economic value of the grain itself. Various estimates could be made, but it costs anywhere from 15 to 20 cents a bushel to carry grain from one year to the next. So if we are going to allow the grain to stay in the country rather than following an aggressive policy of selling grain it will only be a matter of five or six years until we, as a nation, will have sustained the loss of the value of that grain, because the value will have been eaten up by the burdensome carrying charges and interest charges.
The Export Credits Insurance Act has been of some value in the past, but I dp not think it can possibly be the answer. As a matter of fact I do not think it is the answer even in the restricted field to which it applies, because we know that under this act the government has provided for the advance of credit on a rather short-term basis. Export Credits Insurance Act United States had last year when it sold more than twice as much wheat as Canada sold, some 540 million bushels as compared with Canadian sales of 260 million bushels. Mr. Chairman, I can give the assurance that as soon as the resolution stage is completed the bill will be brought down as soon as it is possible for the printers


to print the date on the bill. It would then be distributed immediately, within a matter of a few hours. As a matter of fact, I could distribute some of the preliminary copies of which I have a few to the leaders of the various parties as soon as we complete the resolution stage.
I appeal to hon. members to follow the course of action which has been suggested by the right hon. member for Melville. I think it would be a great advantage if the bill were in the hands of hon. members, farm organizations, farmers and other interested parties so that all could study it and see what it contains. It would avoid a great deal of discussion on what you might call false trails if this were done.
It seems to me there is a lot of genuine misconception in the minds of many people as to what this bill proposes to do and what it contains. Therefore, the sooner it gets into the hands of people who are interested the sooner they will be in a position to assess what the bill actually contains and what it is possible to accomplish under it.
There are two basic misconceptions which I should perhaps mention. There seems to be the idea in the minds of many people that what I called the basic security feature of the bill, that is the provision that under no circumstances should the prices for certain key commodities be allowed to go below 80 per cent of the base price, was a provision that the only thing provided was 80 per cent of the average price which has prevailed during the preceding three years. I know a lot of people have seized on that as though it were the only feature in the bill, as though it were the only thing it contained and as though it were the main feature of the bill. It is not the main feature of the bill at all, Mr. Chairman, it is just an ultimate security measure written into the legislation so that farmers will never again be in the position such as they have been in the past where the prices fell to half of what they were, fell very rapidly to a fraction of what they had been or some other very drastic decline like that. That is the sole purpose of that part of the bill, the basic security feature of the bill.
The main part of the bill, actually the important part of the bill, is the provision to provide for a guaranteed yearly price on commodities as those prices may be required. Now I think a good deal of the criticism which has been made in the house and which as a result has got into the newspapers and I think given people incorrect ideas is that because a three-year moving average is used as a formula in the bill to determine the base price, and because of the

fact that during the past three years the average prices have not been satisfactory as far as many farmers are concerned, this means that the yearly guaranteed prices as set out in the bill are going to be extremely low, and so on. That is not so at all. The base price, based on the three-year moving average, is the particular type of formula employed because it is the only formula under which you can have a really flexible price support program.
Any price support program which attempts to use as its formula a base period in the past and apply an index to it, and so forth, immediately gets you into a rigid formula. I think the experiences of all countries in the world demonstrate the fact that a rigid formula just does not work. In that connection I think perhaps it might be interesting to give a couple of paragraphs from a preliminary report on the food and agriculture meetings in Rome which were concluded only two or three weeks ago. When a cow is bred the farmer should know what he is going to get for the calf three years hence or it is not a forward price. When he breeds the cow he will then know exactly what he will get for the steer or the heifer on the hoof at such and such a time. A year may be all right for sheep or hogs but when it comes to cattle it is no good whatever. You have got to have at least three years. I hope the minister will take that into consideration.
I have a lot of friends in the House of Commons and I talk to them about different things. Many of them are against controls. If you are going to bring in a workable support price policy there will have to be controls. I have never been against controls. During the war we had controls and our farmers got a better share of the national income than they got either before or since. The producer, the packer and the consumer all got a fair pound of flesh in turning the live animal into food.
Look at the beef we produce. Look at the hogs we produce. We did produce millions of pounds of pork and, may I say, the finest pork in the world today. There is nothing to beat Canadian bacon. That is the way I like controls. Everybody gets a square deal and, as I said, during the war our farmers got a better share of the national income than they have before or since.
I hope the minister will tell us what use he is going to make of the experimental farms in order to advise the farmer as to how much it should cost him to produce animals. That is their business. You do not need to grab

If you will then allow the farmer his wages he will be satisfied because at the present time he sometimes does not get the price of the feed he puts into the animal.
I do not know what you are going to do about cattle. Today you have steers up to 1,000 pounds in choice, good, medium and common grades. You have steers over 1,000 pounds in choice, good, medium and common. You have heifers in good, medium and common. You have cows in good, medium and common and you also have canners and cutters. Then you have replacement cattle. You have calves. How are you going to set the prices for them? Are you going to establish a board of livestock commissioners like the board of grain commissioners in order to do that job and to see that the farmer gets a square deal under the price policy?
I have mentioned the various grades. The only thing that the housewife buys is beef. There are nine or ten grades of cattle and the only thing she buys is beef. There are nine grades of pork including "A" hogs, No. 1 sows, No. 2 sows, heavy and extra heavy. A housewife does not go into a butcher shop and ask for a piece of No. 1 sow or extra heavy. She asks for a leg of pork. The thing is ridiculous. I hope the minister is going to be able to straighten it out in a way that it has never been done before.
I have other friends in the House of Commons who say to me, "Scottie, if you got your way you would take away the independence of the farmer." My goodness, what independence has the farmer left today? When he sells his hogs what does he do? He gets hold of a trucker, loads the hogs on the truck and tells the trucker to take them to a certain packing company. What does the farmer do? He sits at home and waits until the cheque comes. When I first came to this country about 40 years ago the farmer had some say in the sale of his produce but today he has absolutely no say in what should be done. The hogs are taken to the packing plant, he never sees them again and he gets a cheque. If he is satisfied he is one of the lucky ones. If he is dissatisfied there is nothing he can do about it.
I read the minister's remarks in Hansard when he used eggs as an example. As found at page 2187 of Hansard of December 11, he said:
Let us say that the average wholesale price of eggs in 1954 was 45 cents a dozen. In 1955 it was

The example which the minister gave us was a rising market, but if it had been a falling market just imagine where we would be. I have to do a lot of thinking about this 80 per cent of parity, but if eggs were 60 cents then, as I understand it, you would only get 80 per cent of that, so you would only get 48 cents a dozen for the eggs. There is no parity at all, but I am giving the minister the benefit of the doubt. I do not want to fall out with the man.

I must say that the hon. member for Selkirk was well worth listening to; I am sure we all enjoyed him. Quite a number of the points he mentioned are things which have nothing to do with a price support measure. They were marketing and grading problems and are not directly related to a measure of this kind.
Now, the only reason I am on my feet again, Mr. Chairman, is that the hon. member has not understood my explanation. I must apologize for the fact the explanation was not clear as to the various types of prices mentioned by me in introducing this resolution. I should like to make the point that the base price is arrived at by taking the average of prices for three years previous, and is used the same as a foot rule is used in measuring length. In other words, it is a measuring device to a large extent and therefore one should not try to put a great deal of emphasis on the particular type of measuring device. In some other support price formulae you take a base period, we will say as it is in the United States, from 1910 to 1914, then you apply an index to it; you apply another index and so forth and eventually you arrive at something that not one farmer in a thousand is able to understand. While this system might appear complicated, I can assure you it is a marvel of simplicity in comparison with some of these support price formulae and plans. In any event, the purpose of that base price is really


to serve as a measuring device, to give you something to which to relate the actual price set. In other words, just as you would use a foot rule to measure distance, you use the base price to a considerable extent and you arrive at it by applying the three-year moving average formula, as something to which to tie the other price.
Perhaps I could put it this way so the hon. member would understand it better. There are two types of support provided for at two different levels altogether. There is, as I said before, the ultimate security feature, the fact that written right into the measure is a provision that, so far as certain basic commodities are concerned, they must be supported at all times at 80 per cent of the base price. We have never said this base price was parity. I do not want any misconception in anyone's mind that I am trying to maintain the base price is a parity price. I have never said so. I have never attempted to convince anybody of that fact.

They seem to be concerned with trying to confuse the issue instead of trying to enable people who do not understand what the measure provides to get a clear picture in their minds. This is a mandatory floor price which is provided for right in the bill, and it must be in effect at all times, that is, 80 per cent of these base prices. As I say, that is what you might call the ultimate security measure in the bill. Then the bill provides for the setting of yearly guaranteed support prices. As I said a little while ago, that is really the important feature of the bill. I would hope hon. members would not continue to talk of this bill as though it provided for 80 per cent of the average of the last three years, and so forth, because that is absolutely incorrect.

It depends upon what the hon. member for Acadia means. It is the only absolute guarantee written into the legislation, yes, but the important thing is this, there is also the guarantee that the legislation provides, as I say, for the setting of these yearly prices, and that is the forward pricing feature which has been requested for many years. I would like to say further that you cannot have both your cake and eat it. If you want, and if the farmers want a rigid price support formula then they have to accept the fact that only a very limited number of products can be or will be supported.

That is the situation in the United States. They produce in that country 250 different farm commodities. How many of those commodities are under price support in the United States? I will tell you how many-thirteen, that is all. Thirteen commodities, plus dairy products and wool. That is the position this year. Of all the commodities which are produced in the United States only 13 are under price support. As a result of that rigid type of price support policy, four-fifths of all the money which is paid out for the price support program went to one-quarter of the farmers. Only one-quarter of the farmers secured four-fifths of all the money paid out.
Now if you attempt to apply a rigid price support program you immediately run into this difficulty, and it exists not only in the United States but in every other country which has tried it or which has it in effect. You can only support a very limited number of commodities. If you want a system under which you can support every farm commodity you must go to a flexible price support program, and that is what we have done as far as this is concerned.
We wanted to have a program under which you could have a support for every agricultural product produced in Canada and the only way in which you can do that is by means of a flexible program of this type or some other type of flexible thing, a program such as we are proposing to put into effect. As I say, if people talk and continue to talk about a fixed price formula-a rigid formula-it means they are actually talking about trying to support the prices of just a very few commodities. The only way in which you can support every commodity is under some flexible type of program.

There is no rigid formula, no. You are getting back to this idea of a rigid formula again. There is no rigid formula which they must follow but here are the factors which they would use in arriving at this formula: (a) estimated cost of production on the average efficient farm; (b) supply of commodity; (c) prospective domestic and export outlets for it; (d) price levels at which other commodities are being supported. In other words we want to have some relation, which has not existed in the past, between the price support, say on hogs, and the price support on dried skimmed milk or anything else.
Then there are: (e) historical price information; (f) disposal and storage problems. In other words a commodity which is extremely perishable and for which there are no storage facilities you could not support at the same level at which you could support a commodity, such as butter, which can be stored quite readily for long periods and for which there are storage facilities. Then: (g) perishability of the commodity-another very important factor-(h) the length of production cycle-which is the matter the hon. member for Selkirk mentioned-(i) the availability of funds; (j) the number of producers affected. Of course with a commodity in which very few producers are affected, you could if you wanted to, support it at a very much higher level than you could support a commodity in which there were millions of producers, or it might be better to say hundreds of thousands of producers. Then, (k) the regional nature of the problem. You

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to go along with the minister's suggestion that we get through this resolution stage as quickly as possible so that we may have a look at the bill. There are, however, a number of things I should like to say which could appropriately be said at this stage. Last Wednesday, was, I think, a sad day for the people of Canada who are dependent on agriculture for their livelihood. Many hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Acadia, clearly showed why the agricultural industry needs some solid, workable and helpful legislation now. I am not going to go over that ground again on this resolution stage. However, members from many parts of the house have indicated disappointment with the explanation of the resolution given by the Minister of Agriculture, or perhaps I should say not with the minister's explanation but with the contents of that explanation. I am afraid that individual farmers and farmer organizations are also feeling the pangs of disappointment. There is one thing I think we should remember, and that is that if we are disappointed now we had better brace ourselves for what is still to come. Only a few short weeks ago we had another resolution before us, and at that time, from the minister's explanation we thought we had a fairly good bill. I am speaking, of course, of the bill in regard to cash advances. But when the bill was brought in, what a disappointment it proved. It was tied up and tangled up with conditional regulations so that very little genuine assistance was provided for grain producers. In that regard I have a news report here from the Lethbridge Herald which is headlined: "No Rush in South for Cash Advances". If the bill which is to follow this resolution is to be a disappointment in relation to the resolution to the same degree as the bill following the cash advances resolution was, then, as I said, brace yourselves.
This resolution is in my opinion, not materially different in any way from what we have already in the statute book, and if anything it will be of even less help because it exempts things such as oats and barley which the prices support act in chapter 3 did not exempt. We will have to wait to see the bill, but if this is supposed to be part of the Conservative program to see that agriculture gets its fair share of the national income, then I think this legislation can be summed up in

one sentence by saying that the Conservatives must be of the opinion that agriculture has already got too much.
This brings up the question of what we in the opposition should do about this legislation. I think we have several alternatives. In the first place, possibly, we should get this into law as soon as possible so that the farmers may be able to see and judge for themselves the weaknesses of this Conservative policy. On the other hand, we should try, possibly, to stop it or to delay as much as possible so that the government may not feel that it has discharged its obligation to agriculture. However, I think that in the interest of agriculture we should possibly try to prevent this from superseding what is already on the statute books, because weak as that agricultural bill is it appears to me that it is better than this one.
The minister has said we do not understand this measure but I am sure we understand it only too well. If it only provides 80 per cent of what is already too little, I see no advantage in passing it at all. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says this is possibly another case of delayed action to get the Conservatives past the next election. Just for one minute I should like to make some comparisons between the minister's explanations of the resolution and what we already have on the statute books. In section 9 it says this under the heading "Powers of the Board":
To prescribe from time to time, with the approval of the governor in council, prices at which the board may purchase agricultural products in the market.
I should like the minister to explain to me whether that is materially different from what he has called forward prices. They already have the power to establish forward prices if they wish to do so. And further down, it reads:
(c) To pay to the producers of an agricultural product directly, or through such agent as the board may determine, the difference between a price prescribed by the board with the approval of the governor in council for such product and the average price, as determined by the board, at which such product is sold in the market during a specified period if such average price is below such prescribed price.
It seems to me now that having brought in this three year formula, why, they could use a three year formula or a two year formula or any other which seemed desirable. They already have the power to set up prices on the basis of any formula they wish. But there is one thing in this act about which I have heard nothing from the minister, and that is the provision at the bottom which says:
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
The board will endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.
Perhaps I have not followed too closely, but I have not yet seen anything which the minister has indicated that it is going to have any relation to the gross national product or to the fair share of the national income.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I say once again that I do not wish to delay this bill. I think however, the time has come and if the Conservatives want to rattle their sabres about something which "will not be too long delayed" this might be a good measure on which to go to the people.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased to exercise my parliamentary responsibility and express my views and the views of my constituents on this resolution.
Before doing so I should like to ask the government the cause of the delay between the time this legislation was placed on the order paper and the time we received it in the house. It was forecast in the speech from the throne nearly two months before the day on which it was brought down in spite of repeated requests by hon. members of this group for early action on this legislation.
This delay would have been unnecessary if the election promises made by the Conservative government that they would call a session in September to deal with this as a matter of urgency had been fulfilled. I think, Mr. Chairman there is a close analogy between this situation and the situation concerning the arrival of a circus in town. First, there is terrific advance press publicity. We had all that during the election campaign. The farmers were promised prices which would give them a fair share of the national income. Advertising was put out, and the prospects displayed on most attractive posters. After that, we had a resolution placed on the order paper which adds to the interest and to the expectation. And then, in addition, we had the spieler in the form of the Minister of Agriculture giving us the come-on. I was not as impressed by the come-on spiel as I was with the resolution, and I think the minister would have done better and would have drawn a bigger crowd if there had been no explanation at all, because it seems to me he gave away some of the secrets of the show, and some of us now might hesitate about buying a ticket to go in.
However, I think the problem facing us is the resolution rather than the explanation of the minister and it does promote considerable
2400	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization interest. There should be strong criticism levelled at the government for its delay in bringing in a measure to offer relief to the crisis in agriculture because of the present conditions. It is apparent that over the past number of years a similar charge of delay has been levelled at governments and I call as my witness the then hon. member for Lake Centre, the present Prime Minister, speaking on July 29, 1944, as reported at page 5599 of Hansard when the Agricultural Prices Support Act was introduced. He said:
One observation I would make at the beginning is that it is passing strange that legislation as important as this should have been been brought down so late in the session.
Those are the views of the present Prime Minister. He continued:
When one considers-that it is introduced on a Saturday in the dying days of the session when by reason of long hours of sitting during the week members are necessarily tired out and unable to give the bill as much attention as it should receive, it seems only right that protests should be made against this sort of procedure.
Mr. Chairman, do we not have a repetition of those same circumstances which were condemned by the Prime Minister on that occasion? I would like now to place on the record the words of the hon. member for Huron in the same debate in relation to the Agricultural Prices Support Act as reported at page 5598 of Hansard who said:
If it is being brought in only for election purposes, of course it will do no good. If it is an honest attempt to do what it purports to do, then I support it wholeheartedly. Something of this kind is long past due.

speechtext: Was that his only speech?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
It was not a very long one but I appreciate the thought that it involved.
The purpose of the debate on the resolution stage is to give the government the advice and the thinking of the house on the proposed legislation. The present Minister of Agriculture has declared himself to be an authority on this subject and to know just as much about it as any hon. member in the chamber but I think there are many hon. members who are not familiar with all agricultural conditions in Canada and in the hope that these views will be given consideration in the proposed bill I would like to make a review of agricultural conditions.


It has been stated in previous debates that agriculture finds itself in a depressed condition at the present time due to the reduction of the net farm income. It was pointed out that from 1952 to 1956 there has been a decline of the net farm income in Canada of 18 per cent and in my own province of Saskatchewan this decline has been 31 per cent. I think perhaps I should explain the term "net farm income". It is the money we as farmers have left after paying our costs of operation. We do not know yet what will be the net farm income for 1957 but there is every indication that it will be about half the net farm income for 1956. We can see indications of that because from January to June of this year there has been a decline of $8 million in cash farm income, which is the total receipts of farmers in Canada as a whole, and in Saskatchewan we find in that same period a decline of 10 per cent.
In the debate on cash advances on farm-stored grain when this problem was dealt with it was pointed out that it is necessary to give serious consideration to what is generally referred to as the cost-price squeeze. This refers to the tremendous increase in our costs of production and the decline in the prices we receive. In the last ten years there has been a decline in the wheat price of 21 per cent whereas the cost of production has gone up 46 per cent. I am certain that the same cost-price squeeze affects farmers in all parts of Canada whether they reside in Quebec, Ontario, the Atlantic provinces, British Columbia or in the western provinces. They are all plagued with the same problem.
I want to look more specifically at the problems of my own constituency of Kindersley and bring them to the attention of the committee because I feel they are representative of the problems in western Canada in particular. It is difficult to obtain authoritative evidence of the cost of production because there are no government publications which give an exact indication. However, the experimental farm service has surveyed wheat production costs and they provide some information which will be of interest to all hon. members. The Manitoba Co-operator of May 2, 1957, in reporting on the review of the experimental farm service says:
In 1956. the average cost of producing wheat on summerfallow on 10 illustration station farms amounted to $23.22 per acre. The factors of production considered in this study, and the percentage (in brackets) each contributed to the total cost per acre are as follows: Rent of land, taxes and use of buildings $208 per acre (9.0 per cent); cost of summerfallow, plus interest $6.51 (28.0 per cent); seeding, preparation and cost of seed, $4.94 (21.3 per cent); fertilizer, spraying and hail insurance, $1.91	(8.3 per cent); harvesting operations, $4.89
(21.1 per cent); interest on net cost at 3 per cent

on seed, fertilizer and labour $0.16 (0.7 per cent); general equipment charge, $0.51 (2.2 per cent); general farm expenses, $1.06 (4.4 per cent); and a management charge of $1.16 (5.0 per cent).
I believe it is important that these figures be given consideration because they reveal the tremendous increase in the cost of production over the years and should serve to give hon. members from every part of Canada an appreciation of the problems the wheat farmer is facing.
In that same connection I must express disappointment that in explaining the resolution the minister mentioned that wheat, oats and barley coming under the Canadian wheat board were specifically excluded from the operation of the system anticipated by this resolution. I was hoping in reading the original resolution that these commodities would be included since there is certainly a strong demand to have these basic commodities included.
To continue with evidence indicating the plight of farmers I would turn to the annual report of the Kindersley vocational agriculture farm management program. This is a program which works in connection with the larger school unit in that district and is based on a survey of 69 farms in the area. This annual report indicates that the cost of production per crop acre including no wage to the operator is $21 per acre as an average on all farms. Including a $3,000 operator wage, which is very moderate in this day and age, the cost would be $28 per acre as an average for all farms. We can readily see the impossible battle the western farmer is waging in meeting his cost of production when the Minister of Trade and Commerce has admitted that all we can expect this year is a six-bushel quota. On the basis of half summerfallow this would give 12 bushels per wheat acre provided you had no special crops which reduced the quota. This, at the very most, would give you a return of $15 a crop acre. I have already pointed out that the cost of production is $21 per acre.
It is more than evident that the farmers are having to live on the depreciation costs of their farm machinery. The Canadian Journal of Agricultural Economics, in a study of the depreciation charges per crop acre, pointed out that for a 320-acre farm the cost is $4.53; on a section farm it is $3.99; and on a 2-section farm, $3.07. Therefore, more than the depreciation which farmers should normally be allowed to put aside for the replacement of their equipment is being completely utilized in order to continue the operation of the farms. As a result of that, I
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization noticed in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of November 28, 1957, an article entitled: Bleak Outlook
Lloyd Barber, professor of commerce at the University of Saskatchewan, said Wednesday there was a bleak outlook for the farm implement retail business.
The article goes on to say:
In the next two decades it was possible that where three dealers were operating now there might be only business for one.
There, Mr. Chairman, is evidence which I think is irrefutable to give to hon. members a full appreciation of the agricultural conditions which are facing farmers in western Canada, and I maintain the same circumstances apply to farmers in other parts of Canada. It points out the need for action on the part of this government to forestall this trend. It is apparent that it is not just the farmer who is suffering because these circumstances apply to all those in the smaller communities and in the larger communities who have direct contact with the farmer.
I pointed out that the article indicates a very , bleak future for the implement dealers. Those hon. members who have travelled through rural Canada will appreciate the number of implement dealers who will be put in jeopardy. It applies, of course, to all services to the farmer, to the municipalities and counties.
As I have pointed out, the rising costs are not being offset by the very low deliveries of grain from the farm. As of November 25, which are the latest figures available, it is indicated that there are 644 marketing points still on the unit quota. They are allowed to deliver only 300 bushels of wheat and a fixed proportion of other grains. There are 1,133 marketing points on a 1-bushel quota and only 263 marketing points on a 2-bushel quota. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, it is apparent that agriculture is facing a dilemma. The same situation certainly applies to those who are in other forms of enterprise.
It has been asked many times by those who have not been adequately informed: Why do you keep on growing wheat when there is obviously no market for it? Why do you not grow something else? In fact, the Minister of Trade and Commerce in that speech he made in Winnipeg implied the same thing. Well, we have the alternative of farmers transferring to other grains, and there has been a great transfer to the growing of durum, which has a very limited market. What will happen as we transfer from the growing of spring wheat to durum wheat is that we shall in turn glut that market.
The market for flax is a doubtful one although the seedings have gone up over 150
2402	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization per cent from the previous year and it is questionable just how much the market can absorb. The third alternative which the farmers have been following is the growing of rape seed, and we find that we are confronted with an exorbitant freight rate and as yet the government has taken no action to dissallow the decision which was made by the board of transport commissioners granting the increase and thus give the farmers a fair deal on that, although they have the privilege and the responsibility. Here again the production of rape seed is limited. You cannot turn all of your acreage into the production of those other crops. I maintain that the farmers have co-operated because the acreage seeded to wheat has dropped in the province of Saskatchewan over a million acres in the last three years.
Well, we have another alternative, namely to transfer to livestock, and I think it is important that this be given consideration in discussing a resolution to provide stability to agriculture. In the first instance, the cash outlay to transfer to livestock from a grain operation is tremendous. I have a letter from a veteran in my constituency, Mr. Timothy McBride of Marengo, who found himself with a large surplus of wheat and who wanted to transfer to livestock. He is a settler under the Veterans' Land Act. He will not get title to his land until May 31, 1959. He would need $5,000 to buy a herd of cattle and to set up the buildings to house them, but he cannot get the money because in the first place he has no title to his land; but, more pointedly, there is no credit policy in Canada to give assistance to such a man who is trying to resolve this problem.
Of course, there are other problems related to the transfer to livestock. One that I would cite would be the shortage of feed and the shortage of water. I am quite familiar with this, Mr. Chairman, because on my own farm I have run a fairly large herd of cattle over the past number of years. 1 had at the start of this year 85 head of cattle and I found that because of the very meagre moisture supply that we had my pastures were drying up. I had to sell 20 head of those cattle and it was fortunate I did because in the course of the year my three dugouts dried up and the two wells which I have to supply those cattle with water are on the verge of going dry any day. Therefore, we have to give very serious consideration to the blanket suggestion that we should transfer to livestock.
In addition to this, members from eastern Canada should be aware of the impact which it would have on their economy if indeed the farmers of western Canada were to transfer to livestock in great numbers. The traditional


tendency has been for the western feeder cattle to be transported to Ontario and Quebec where they are finished off for the large eastern market. In western Canada we have the cattle and we have the feed, and I would submit we would be transferring the problem to the eastern farmers if the farmers in western Canada were to go extensively into livestock.
Now, I should like to make some suggestions which would, in my opinion, resolve this basic problem and they should be given consideration in this resolution. It has been stated by the president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool that the income of western farmers must be increased to meet the cost of production. I think we have an important point there which must be given consideration in this resolution.
In the remarks he made the minister indicated that there is no direct relationship between the cost of production and the base price established under this legislation. If that is the case, it is a very serious omission, indeed, because the cost of production and the prices must bear a relationship which will give the farmer a fair return.
One of the short-term proposals which I would suggest to resolve this lack of income would be the payment of a domestic parity price for wheat to the farmers of western Canada. It has been pointed out that over the years, particularly in the early war years, the farmers of western Canada subsidized all of the people in Canada by taking a low price for their wheat; and even today the farmers are getting much less than their cost of production of wheat. Therefore, it would naturally follow that the price of wheat should be increased to the farmer to bear some relationship to the cost of production. It would not increase the price of bread by an appreciable amount, since there is only three cents worth of wheat in a loaf of bread at the present time. On 50 million bushels, which is the amount consumed domestically, it would mean about $25 million to the farmers of western Canada which should be distributed to assist the smaller farmer.
In addition, other producers in Canada who are receiving a price less than their cost of production must receive a deficiency payment. This is not a subsidy. It is an economic technique which would provide those farmers with the money whereby they could meet their cost of production. If they do not meet their cost of production Canada will be confronted not only with an economic but a sociological problem because as farmers go bankrupt and have to move from the farm they in turn create other problems elsewhere in industry.

The proposal of deficiency payments has been advocated by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the interprovincial farm union council and is accepted by farmers. I am hopeful that the principle will be encompassed in the legislation although I am afraid the minister let the cat out of the bag in his explanation and that the principle will not be covered.
We must also give consideration to additional long-term policies which will solve the dilemma of agriculture. We must remove some of the shackles of trade barriers so that Canadian agricultural products can be exported. We must give further consideration to purchasing goods from the United Kingdom so that they in turn will be in a position to buy goods from us. We must face the problem of providing agricultural credit. At the turn of the century agriculture was an expanding industry and all of the policies of this country were geared to an expanding industry. We can think of the settlement policy whereby the government bet the farmer $10 against a quarter section of land that he could not last there for a year. The whole thing was aimed at expanding agriculture. But now that we have mechanization, now that we have $7,000 combines that can do more than several threshing outfits, it is necessary to give consideration to that fact in our agricultural policy and provide policies for readjustment so that farmers can in turn form themselves into an economic unit.
The minister admitted that the legislation was inadequate to meet many of these conditions. I think that admission is rather an indictment of the measure because surely to goodness on the basis of the election promises and the hopes that were raised in people's minds this measure should have solved at least some of the basic problems. In order to resolve the dilemma of agriculture the legislation must include a relationship between the cost of production and the prices paid.
The minister has made a great point of the flexibility of the legislation, how it can be moved about, but it looks to me like this flexibility is going to be a rubber hose with which the farmers will be beaten over the head. The flexibility is not related to any particular subject at all and the minister has complained about rigidity.
In addition, the minister has pointed out that the purpose of the legislation is to guarantee prices. For how long? For one year? A guaranteed price for one year is useless because it does not take into consideration the production cycles in certain industries. It would be all right if you were
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization growing peas. You could plant them in the spring and harvest them in the fall and you would be assured of your price.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: And mushrooms.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Kootenay West suggests mushrooms. That is something else to which help might be given in an effective way. A one-year guaranteed forward price is of no value to the poultryman because in his case there is a two-year production cycle. What about the man who decides to transfer to the production of hogs? In that case there is a three-year production cycle. Of what value is it to him to know that in one specific year he has a guaranteed price? What about the cattle producer? In that case there is a five-year production cycle. Is one year the best the government can do to provide stability for agriculture? We must have a forward price based on the production cycle if the farmer is going to be assured any degree of security and stability.
In addition, the agricultural program must ensure that agriculture receives a fair share of the national income. That is implied in the resolution but unfortunately in giving his explanation the minister indicated that this was something that would be in the discretion of the government. I think it should go beyond that. There are other measures that should accompany this one in order to meet the needs of Canadian agriculture.
As I mentioned, we must have adequate credit facilities to assist young farmers to become established because failing that and with the present cost-price squeeze they are drifting away from this useful and essential occupation to other occupations which they perhaps may not enjoy. We must have a crop insurance program to supplement this measure.
I have dealt in some detail with many of the problems confronting agriculture. I hope I have been able to convince hon. members of the extreme need that exists in Canada for a realistic agricultural policy to provide stability for the family farms. If the measure does not include recommendations to meet these problems, I suggest that the minister should whisk it back for redrafting and in any case he should refer it to the agriculture committee of the House of Commons so that farm organizations and members of the house may be able to make a workable proposition out of it.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think one of the needs of the house is for some member to stand up and speak of the joys of the farm. I should like to do so but I do not

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization want to take too much time on this resolution. However, may I suggest one or two. Look at the joy of exploring the mysteries of a farm, why a red cow will eat green grass and give white milk. Tell me why it is that taking two grains of wheat of the same size and the same weight one will germinate sooner than the other and one will produce two stalks and the other will produce three. Look at the little chicks, the lambs, the kids, the colts, the joy of experimenting and producing better potatoes.
The farmers of the Fort William district are not living in starvation. In our community we have the champion potato grower and there are others who are experimenting with oats. If we want to help the farmers, let us pass the resolution and get the bill.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are discussing a measure to provide guaranteed prices for certain commodities. I think this is probably one of the most important pieces of legislation-the Minister of Agriculture himself has said so-that has come before the house during this session at least. I think it would be wrong if members of the house did not avail themselves of the opportunity to do everything they could in order to make the legislation better than it now appears to be.
In discussing the measure the only thing we have on which to base our judgment is what the minister said in his speech and I must take it for granted that what the minister did say was based on the bill itself. True there are not too many who know anything about the bill. There has not been too much consultation with others in drafting the bill so we must rely on what the minister has told us. Therefore, I assume that what the minister said in his speech about the resolution is correct.
There have been a great many people throughout this country who have been quite concerned about this proposed measure. Within the last few days there has been a great deal of publicity given to it. Whether or not the government delayed the introduction of this measure in order to get this advance publicity, I cannot say, but certainly that was the result.
Within the last little while the minister has been urging us to pass this measure; hurry up and get it through. I do not believe the members of this house should rush a bill of this kind-

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: A resolution.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
-or a resolution, because it is something that is going to materially affect the economic condition, not

only of the farmers in Canada but all of the people in Canada. The effects of it are going to last for a number of years. I am sure there is no farmer in this country who would not say to his member of parliament, do not rush this thing through; take all the time that is necessary and see if you cannot make some improvements on this otherwise unfavourable measure. The minister does not want to take too much for granted because there are a number of people in this country who are very concerned about this measure.
Mention has been made before during this debate, and I just recall it again to the minister's mind, that some very definite promises were made during the election campaign. There were some definite promises made by the Conservative candidate in my constituency, and by others who spoke over the radio and over the T.V. from Calgary, as to what would be done for the farmers if the Conservatives were elected.
I am not going to refer to newspaper clippings, but I want to refer to a resolution that was passed by one of the farm organizations in my constituency, a district in which some Conservatives spoke and in which the Prime Minister himself spoke. This is a resolution from the farmers' union of Alberta in Carbon, local 1005, and which was sent to me a short time ago. It is addressed to me, and reads:
Whereas during his campaign, if he formed the government, the present Prime Minister J. G. Diefenbaker said, "We will assure the farmer of his fair share of the national income by maintaining a flexible price support program. X underline the word flexible-"
The Prime Minister is still speaking.
'*-to ensure an adequate parity for agricultural producers, based on a fair price-cost relationship- My pledge to farmers in all parts of Canada is; to assure that the farmer shall receive his fair share of the national income."
That is the end of the quotation from the Prime Minister, and then it goes on:
Therefore, be it resolved that Mr. Charles E. Johnston, M.P., keep constantly in front of the Prime Minister and the government, the promises made by Mr. Diefenbaker prior to the last election, stressing the price support program, and of the farmer receiving his fair share of the national income.
Now Mr. Chairman, that is exactly what I am doing and what I intend to do. I believe that any member in this house, be he Conservative, Liberal, Social Credit or C.C.F., would not be serving his constituents if he neglected to keep that pledge in this house, and express here on the floor the same comments that he made out on the hustings. I believe there has been only one Conservative in this debate so far who has said he approves of this measure in its present form, and the bill which will follow.

Let me start now to discuss the speech made by the Minister of Agriculture the other day. He pointed out to us that this legislation implemented all their election promises. I do not want to take anything for granted, so I will turn to page 2816 of Hansard for December 11, 1957, and there I find he said this:
The resolution before us is one on which a bill will be based that is designed to put into effect our stated program of greater stability of income for agriculture.
Then, he goes on:
This is a far-reaching and important piece of legislation,-
It certainly is far-reaching.
-perhaps the most important, in its implications,-
Again I agree with him.
-in its expected results for agriculture and its effect on the general economy, that has been considered by the Canadian parliament for many years.
That is just what I am afraid of, that the effect this measure is going to have on the general economy of Canada is going to be very detrimental to agriculture. Then, again at page 2189 of Hansard, the minister has this to say:
I think this legislation will do everything we promised we would do so far as our campaign pledges are concerned.

Mr. Chairman, and members of the House of Commons, I appreciate the fact that it is possibly the duty of the opposition to try to depict such measures as are now before the house in the blackest manner they can, but I do appreciate the opportunity of speaking at this time in support of the resolution.
I understand that this measure proposes to support and stabilize the products of agriculture. Such a measure, I believe, is necessary and in fact long overdue.
I have many and varied agricultural problems in my own constituency, perhaps more than in any part of Canada. I say this honestly because there are greater variations in the crops produced in Lambton-Kent and therefore there is a greater variety of problems in connection with those crops. I believe that our agricultural policy is unsound and unfair and has been so for a long period of time, and while it must be admitted that there have been times over the past number of years when agriculture has enjoyed a considerable degree of prosperity those times in the main have been brought about by luck rather than planning or management either on the part of the government or of the people.
When I say that these periods of prosperity have been brought about by luck I do not necessarily mean that they have come about as a result of good luck; rather, in large part, they have come about as a result of the worst kind of bad luck which could befall any people, namely war. Surely, Mr. Chairman, there is a better and less costly way of correcting the ills of agriculture than having to resort to war or having to wait for a war to correct them. I am sure we are all in agreement that a small part of the cost of defending ourselves in time of war would correct most of the ills of agriculture in peacetime; yet in wartime we accept the extra load of cost of food together with other costs because then and only then do the people seem to appreciate the vital need and the dependence they have upon agriculture for their very existence.
I have suggested that the position of the farm people appeared to have improved as a result of bad luck befalling the people of the country as a whole in the case of the nation being at war. However, I would like to state here that even that kind of luck has not always worked to the benefit of the farm people in the way they expected it would for I recall quite clearly that during the last war the government of the day saw fit to place price ceilings on agricultural commodities beyond which they could not go and this price ceiling structure had the effect of denying

to people engaged in agriculture the opportunity which would have been afforded in the ordinary course of events to take advantage of a stronger market and at better prices.
Some time ago in speaking in the throne speech debate I mentioned that I had been a member of a delegation which had come to Ottawa asking for measures to protect the sugar beet growers and that we had been refused. Some time later, about the time of the conclusion of the last war, I was again a member of a group of wheat growers who came once more to Ottawa, asking for consideration in the matter of the raising of the price ceiling on wheat which had been set at around $1.12 per bushel. We were not refused on this occasion; in fact, we were well received. We presented our problem and it was gratifying to learn in a few days that the ceiling had been raised to $1.27.
As time passed and the war came to an end farm production costs had continued to rise and the wheat farmers of our area felt that it was unfair to be restricted by a price ceiling that prevented them from taking advantage of the opportunity a free market would have offered them and so another meeting was called and a delegation again came to Ottawa this time to ask that the ceiling be removed entirely and this request was also granted. Shortly after the price rose to the point where it ranged between $2 and $2.40 and where it remained for quite a period of time.
The fact I am endeavouring to point out to hon. members of this committee is that the farm people did carry a big share of the load, perhaps an unjustly large share of the load, in time of war; and if the people and the government feel they had the right to expect the farm people to carry that load in wartime then surely both the people and the government must recognize their responsibility for ensuring that the farmers will share in any measures which will help to keep them in a reasonably sound position in peacetime. I wish to quote from an article that appeared in the Almonte Gazette on November 21, 1957;
We do know that the farmers have very real and obvious grievances. This is indicated by the lamentable trend away from the farms. We noticed in printing the voters' list for Ramsay, this year, that there were 25 fewer names than last year. There was a good reason for us being observant in this connection because printers are paid by the name for printing such lists. But the point is that the most highly assessed township in Lanark county is losing population and has been doing so for many years. There are vacant farms here and there and some of those farms which are still inhabited are being only partially worked, with the men holding down industrial jobs in nearby towns or cities.
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
If agriculture were paid on a scale commensurate with certain other trades or professions, many of them less important, the situation we refer to would not exist. The farmer to a greater extent than any vocation we know of is a prey to weather conditions and many other factors over which he has no control.
I wish now to mention a few of the many other factors that have taken terrific tolls in my time in addition to the question of farm costs and the price of agricultural commodities. Some of these are foot-and-mouth disease in cattle; cholera in hogs; dysentery in poultry; blight and black root rot in sugar beets. Last year many thousands of bushels of white beans were lost on account of excessively wet weather. The wheat growers have to fight the plague of stem rusts, several kinds of smut and the hessian fly. In addition to these the farmer never knows when his crops will be damaged by cut worms, wire worms, army worms and grasshoppers. There are also the problems of excessive freezing and thawing; excessive heat to shrink the grain when ripening; excessive rainfall to prevent harvest, or the other extreme, the lack of rain, to promote growth; wind storms to lodge the grain so it is difficult to obtain, and hail storms that often do tremendous damage.
There is one other thought I wish to leave with hon. members of the committee. I feel that people in lines of business other than agriculture are becoming increasingly aware of the unfavourable position the farmer is placed in and in the main they are fair enough to admit that something should be done about it. They also in the main feel that by assisting agriculture they will indirectly be helping themselves. Therefore, in conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I would emphasize that anything which is done to stabilize the business of agriculture will assist materially in bringing a greater measure of stability to the nation as a whole.
To my mind, Mr. Chairman, the matter before us is something like going to Killarney. You have to start somewhere and it does not matter where you are, the best place is to start from where you are and today that is here. I do not expect this bill is going to be a cure-all for all the ills of agriculture but I would suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that we should try to get the plan in operation; for I believe it does provide an avenue through which at least some of our problems can be solved. Therefore, I say, let us try to make an honest effort to solve the rest as we go along and meet up with them. Mr. Chairman, I have sufficient confidence in the proposals that are before us today to say that
