Mr. Chairman, I think the most important thing that has come to light in this debate, if we can take the statement of the Minister of Agriculture as it is on the record, is the fact that the Conservative government has broken faith with the farmers and the people of this country as far as implementing its commitments, made time and time again during the election to provide a system of parity prices, is concerned. The Prime Minister made it abundantly clear at place after place where they stood in this regard. The Prime Minister went back and forth across this country saying that if he were elected the government would provide a system of parity price supports. I have in my hand a number of statements he made during the election campaign. Let me quote one which appeared in the Regina Leader-Post and which was made at Kipling, where he said that the price of wheat at $1.40 per bushel was too low and should be increased. Another one is a Canadian Press dispatch in the Ottawa Citizen of June 10, 1957, and is a quotation from a speech made in Saskatchewan on June 8. It reads as follows, referring to the Prime Minister:
He promised them that if a Conservative government is elected he will call a September session of parliament to set up a system of floor prices for agricultural produce based on parity.
That was a very definite commitment which has been broken. According to the Regina Leader-Post of May 18, when speaking in Regina, he said this:
I urged a system of parity prices in 1941 in a resolution in the house and asked for it two other times, but every Liberal member voted against it.
I think it is important at this time to quote the motion made by the Prime Minister in this house in 1941, and I quote from Hansard of April 8, 1941, at page 2280:
That all the words after "that" in the motion be struck out, and that the following be substituted therefor:
it be resolved that the government should take immediate steps to create a parity of prices as between agricultural and other products in order to improve the condition of Canadian agriculture and in order that it may receive a just and fair return,-
That is the position taken by the Prime Minister; that is the commitment he made to the people of this country and yet in this legislation that is being discussed at this time, the guaranteed floor below which prices cannot fall is less than the very low prices prevailing at the current period. Conditions now, according to an index of the dominion bureau of statistics based on 1935-39, are worse than they were at that time. I have


the Economic Annalist in my hand and it shows that in the three-year period on which these guaranteed prices are based, in 1955, prices of agricultural prices were 2 per cent less than the index of the cost of production. They were worse in 1955 than in the late 1930's. By 1956, this position had deteriorated until prices of farm products were 7 per cent worse in relation to costs than they were in the late 1930's. At April of this year the index was 11 per cent worse than it was in the late 1930's, and this is the period of prices on which the government is going to base its guarantee to the agricultural producers of this country, its absolute guarantee.
I have in my hand figures showing the average price of hogs at Moose Jaw for the years 1954, 1955 and 1956. It shows that the average price during that 3-year period was $23.28 a hundred. Eighty per cent of that figure is $18.62 a hundred. Although every hon. member will admit that hog prices at the present time are depressed, yet hog prices on the market at Moose Jaw are now in excess of $24 a hundred. The guranteed prices under this legislation are very much lower than the prices prevailing today. If the guaranteed prices, based on the 3-year average, 1954-56, were in effect today for good steers the guaranteed price on the Regina market would be $13.60 and yet the prevailing price is $16.75.
Grain is excluded from the legislation and therefore there is nothing in it for the grain producers of western Canada. The livestock producers find that as far as the floor in this legislation is concerned their position would be much worse than it is at the present time.
The Prime Minister's definite commitments to the people of this country have been broken and this legislation has been a shock to all those people in this country who are interested in the welfare of the farmer. Albert Cormack, who was president of the Ontario farmers union for a number of years, in his fight for parity prices accepted the word of the Conservative government that they meant what they said in the election and was himself, through his organization the farmers union, responsible for the election of a number of hon. members opposite and the defeat of a number of former members of the Liberal government, including the former minister of finance. What was his reaction to this legislation? Here was a man who, because he felt the Conservative party meant what they said, worked for them in the campaign. Mr. Cormack said he received the announcement with a shock, and that is the reaction of farm organizations all across this country. They wonder why the Prime Minister made these definite promises and has waited until

almost Christmas time this session to do anything about them and, on the basis of the minister's statement, is introducing a bill in this house which is a complete violation of those very definite commitments.

Prices in this legislation may be higher than the floor, that is true, but they will be political prices and they will be put up for one year at a time, and the thing next to the heart of the government is any form of legislation to get by the next few months, to get by the next election.
I can tell the Minister of Agriculture why there are no parity prices. I can tell his parliamentary assistant why the minister is against parity prices. If there is anything clear in the record of any hon. member of this house it is the minister's attitude and his record since he came into this house. At every turn he has opposed any suggestion that there should be adequate guarantees for agricultural prices and adequate guaranteed floors under prices.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, statements along this line are at absolute variance with the truth and I do not think the hon. member should be making them. I just cannot understand the hon. member making such statements.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am willing to let the record stand. The trouble is the record is too clear. For instance, when we wanted to get oats and barley under the wheat board so as to have a guaranteed price the minister had this to say, as found at page 1696 of Hansard for February 27, 1948:
I for one-and I know a large number of farmers who feel the same way-do not want to have the government set the price X am to get for oats and barley.
He does not want the government setting prices and the government has not done much in that regard under this legislation. That is the trouble with it. They are offering 80 per cent of the price over a very low, depressed period. In 1954 the hon. member for Mackenzie moved the following resolution, as found at page 4797 of Hansard of May 17: In the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to demonstrating its support of the principle of orderly marketing through livestock marketing boards by announcing floor prices with respect to cattle and hogs at levels not less than the average of the prices which prevailed during the period from January 1, 1951 to December 31. 1953.
96G98-153
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
That would have brought about a floor price for beef of $26.50 a hundredweight and a floor price for B-l hogs at Toronto of $29.65 a hundredweight. This is what the present Minister of Agriculture said in that debate on May 17 as found at page 4806 of Hansard:
In my opinion, if this resolution were put into effect it would be, more or less, complete socialization of the livestock industry.
He is against adequate support prices because he says it is socialism.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: That has got nothing to do with adequate prices.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
He went on to say:
Most livestock producers of whom I am aware do not want their industry socialized.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: That is a rigid price support program you wanted. You still want it and it is not workable. It is a rigid support price program you have been talking about and it is not workable.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: The minister is against anything that is rigid.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: That is not so.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: He does not want a rigid floor. He wants this depressed floor that will do what our friend, Albert Cormack of the farmers union, said it would, drive the farmers off the farms. To make sure that I am not misinterpreting the minister-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Public Works
maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: How about the national president of the farmers union?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
-let me refer to what the minister had to say about an amendment moved by Mr. Bracken on May 6, 1946 with regard to prices of argicultural products. On May 15, 1946, the minister had this to say as found at page 1567 of Hansard:
It is that artificial control of prices and arbitrary distribution of commodities are contrary to the conceptions of free trade and free enterprise-
The present government is against control of prices. This government is against adequate support prices. The minister himself has been the greatest opponent of adequate support prices since he came into the house in 1945.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Again I say that is absolutely untrue.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: The record I have placed on Hansard at this time proves it.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: The record shows nothing of the kind. Nothing that you have read shows it.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister wants to deny it but the legislation before the house is proof positive that he is consistent, and that now

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization he is in office he is doing exactly what he wanted to do when he was in opposition, to have as little to do as possible with government control. Never support adequate floor prices because it would socialize the agricultural industry, he said. The government is not for the agricultural producers of this country. The other day they established a royal commission to inquire into the spread in the prices of agricultural commodities between the price paid to the farmer and the retail price. They appointed a six-man commission and there is not a farmer on it.
I asked the Prime Minister if he had discussed the question of submitting a name or a number of names with the farmers union and the wheat pool and the answer was no. It is an amazing thing that on a royal commission to decide why farmers are getting such low prices in relation to the retail prices of their products the government would not appoint a farmer.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: There are three representatives of agriculture.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
There is no representation of the wheat pools, no representation of the farmers union. It was not even discussed with them. They were brushed aside. The Minister of Agriculture has made it very clear in his presentation to the house that the measure before us will not provide parity prices. It is not aimed at providing parity prices. I have in my hand a copy of a resolution directed to the federal government which reads as follows:
-we urge immediate action by the federal government to implement policies along the lines indicated by the Saskatchewan royal commission on agriculture and rural life with particular reference to:
1.	Price supports for all agricultural products based upon parity and utilizing deficiency payments.
That is the resolution, support prices for agricultural products based on parity and utilizing deficiency payments. Here are some of the organizations that supported this resolution: The Saskatchewan federation of agriculture, Saskatchewan farmers union, Saskatchewan association of rural municipalities, the urban municipalities association, the school trustees association, the co-operative union of Saskatchewan, the Saskatchewan federated co-operatives, the credit union league, the women's co-operative guild, the Saskatchewan agricultural societies association, the Saskatchewan federation of home and school clubs, the Saskatchewan teachers federation, the Saskatchewan home makers club, the rural-municipal secretary-treasurers association of Saskatchewan, the Saskatchewan school unit secretaries association, and the local government continuing committee.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Everybody but the
Saskatchewan Conservatives.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Somebody says, "Everybody but the Saskatchewan Conservatives."

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Public Works
maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: And the Ontario C.C.F.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Following the lead of their party obviously the Saskatchewan Conservatives have abandoned any idea of a system of support prices based on parity. This telegram is a demonstration that Saskatchewan is united in its support of parity prices, that all of these organizations in Saskatchewan are disappointed with the government's legislation which does not provide a system of parity prices based on the cost of production.
Not long ago the Saskatchewan wheat pool passed a resolution at their convention, I understand unanimously, saying that they are prepared to organize a mass delegation to come to Ottawa to impress upon the government that there is a need to provide adequate guarantees to the agricultural industry. This support by all of these organizations in Saskatchewan shows that the day is coming when the people of the country will say to the government in a united way, "We expect and insist that you keep your election promises."

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be very brief but I feel I must say something. A proper price support system for agricultural products based on the cost of production so as to give the farmer his fair share of the national income is a most important issue to the people of my part of the country. Not only is it important, it is vital to their very existence. The ability of this legislation to do that job will determine whether or not the family farm in Canada will continue to exist or will disappear.
For that reason we have welcomed the resolution on the order paper which says that it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish a system of guaranteed prices for certain agricultural commodities to be named therein and to provide that prices may be guaranteed for any other agricultural commodities.
We have supported this and have looked forward to the introduction of this measure. I will say we are very pleased to see the resolution on the order paper. We are rather surprised that the measure has not been bought forward earlier. We had some hope for the legislation until the minister got up the other day and explained one or two things to us with regard to the legislation, which dashed our hopes rather severely.
The first thing he said was that wheat, oats and barley were out; grains were out of the

measure altogether. As Minister of Agriculture he knows how many producers in this country depend upon wheat, oats and barley for their incomes. If these products are beyond the scale of support prices, then how on earth can the minister give any guarantee that these people will get their share of the national income? The minister talked about the base price and the floor price which is 80 per cent of that base price, but that certainly means nothing. If that is all we are going to get as a guarantee, then I can say we look to the legislation with a great deal of scepticism. A great deal will depend upon whether the advisory committee which he sets up will or will not recommend to the government a guaranteed price on farm commodities. We have no assurance that that committee or board will do the job. We have no assurance that if they make a recommendation to the government, the government will carry it through. We are sceptical of measures such as this which say certain things and then they are not carried out.
I have been here long enough to see some of these things in operation. I should like to read to the minister one clause of a bill which was passed in 1945, which was to guarantee farmers against a drop in prices. The minister will know this measure which is called Agricultural Prices Support Act, for the support of the prices of agricultural products during the transition from war to peace. Section 9, subsection 2 of that act reads:
In prescribing prices under paragraphs (a) and (c) of subsection (1) the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.
How much that sounds like the measure we have before us today. How completely that measure failed in its application to do exactly what it was said it would do. Agriculture, in the past number of years has gone down and is in a very depressed condition, not only in the west but in the east as well. Reports from farm areas in Ontario indicate that farmers are unable to carry on their business, even in this province, and make a living. Reports indicate that 50 per cent of the farmers in Ontario are forced to go to industry to supplement their earnings, leaving a wife or a boy at home to try to make the farm pay.
Under the proposed measure arrangements are made for an advisory committee to advise the government as to what it should do. The annual report of the agricultural prices support board contains a repetition each year as to what the board is doing. In each one
96698-153J
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization of the reports the reference to the advisory committee is identical, and I have checked the reports for 1952, 1953, 1954, 1955, 1956 and 1957. The paragraph reads:
The general advisory committee to the board, under the chairmanship of H. H. Hannam, president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, held regular spring and fall meetings. The committee covered a wide field in its discussions and at the conclusion of each meeting submitted a limited number of carefully considered recommendations.
The same recommendations were made, but nothing was done. There was $200 million set aside for a support price program, but they have never used $100 million of it. It costs about $70,000 a year to maintain this board, for salaries and so forth. The money was never used, and that is the reason agriculture is sceptical about this legislation. The government might add another $50,000 to this amount, but if it is not used it does not do much good.
I am not going to say very much more, Mr. Chairman, except that we would like to see the bill. Perhaps the bill will give us more hope than the minister's statement has. Until that time comes, I shall reserve any further comments I have. My confrere, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, says the bill could give little less. We reserve further judgment until the bill is brought down. I can say that if the bill does not mean any more than the minister has indicated in his speech, then we are going to have to fight it because this is a fight for whether or not we will maintain the family farm as part of the Canadian economy.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Harkness thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 237, to establish a system of guaranteed prices for certain agricultural commodities.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
